items.title: Update README and changelog for the inline-value representation
items.body:
Documentation only — no code changes. Brings the README and changelog in line with the inline-value representation merged in #42/#43.

The docs still described the pre-inlining design, and in one place mis-stated the new one:

- The README's technical sections documented the **deleted** 512-entry static integer array, a **2-bit tag with 4-byte alignment**, and a "24-bit heap allocation" for small integers, and stated that arbitrary-precision numbers were **not** supported.
- The README's `INumber` section and the changelog both described inline numbers as an exact decimal (`mantissa * 10^exp`). That is only true with `arbitrary_precision`; **by default the inline slot is a base-2 binary float** (`mantissa * 2^exp`), so every inline number is exactly an `f64`.

## Changes

**README**
- `IValue` technical section: 3-bit tag / 8-byte alignment; seven pointer tags plus the inline family (tag 0), rather than "4 heap types / 2 bits" and the `0x1`/`0x2`/`0x3` constant pointers.
- `INumber` technical + usage sections: inline `mantissa × base^exp` numbers (base 2 by default → always exactly an `f64`; base 10 under `arbitrary_precision` → exact decimal), 56-bit mantissa (24-bit on 32-bit), 8-byte heap spill — replacing the static-array description and the "i8/u8 no-alloc, 24-bit 4-byte-alloc" claims.
- `IString`: short strings are stored inline; longer strings are interned.

**CHANGELOG** (`0.1.7`)
- Fixed the inline-number wording (base-2 binary float by default, not exact decimal).
- Added the missing `arbitrary_precision` feature entry.

items.title: Revamp GeroQuery: real data only, real PhenoAge clock, redesigned UI
items.body:
## Summary

This is a ground-up revamp of GeroQuery that removes all fabricated evidence, rebuilds the tool around **real, cited curated knowledge**, implements the **real published PhenoAge clock**, and rewrites the Streamlit dashboard into a clean, plain-English, gene-first experience.

## Data honesty (the core change)

The previous version generated **fake GEO accessions** (`GSE90001`–`GSE90228`), **synthetic effect sizes**, and **made-up p-values** to fake a "demo meta-analysis," plus a synthetic cohort mislabeled as "NHANES." All of that is gone.

- 🗑️ **Deleted** `signatures.csv`, `studies.csv`, and the mislabeled clinical cohort.
- 🧬 **Added `geroquery/knowledge/`** — a curated, real-evidence knowledge base for the 12 aging genes: direction with age, ordinal confidence (`robust`/`established`/`emerging`, not false-precision numbers), hallmarks of aging, plain-English analysis, per-gene FAQs, and **verifiable PubMed citations** for every claim.
- 📚 **Regenerated** curated database flags (GenAge/CellAge/LongevityMap/OpenGenes) and lifespan interventions (NIA ITP/DrugAge) with primary-source citations.
- 🧪 **Replaced** the demo cohort with `example_cohort_simulated` — 720 synthetic subjects carrying the nine real PhenoAge markers, **clearly labelled `SIMULATED` everywhere** and never presented as real people. Upload-your-own is the first-class path.

## Real biological-age clock

- Implemented the published **Levine PhenoAge** model (`geroquery/clocks/phenoage.py`) with correct unit conversions and the Gompertz mortality transform.
- One model exposes both **biological age (years)** and **10-year mortality risk**, cleanly demonstrating that age and mortality are two facets of one calibrated model.
- Validated numerically: a healthy 40yo → biological age ≈ 28; an unhealthy 70yo → ≈ 84.

## Backend refactor

- `models`/`store`/`sources`/`service`/`api` now serve cited evidence instead of fabricated numeric signatures; gene resolution carries `ortholog_group` for knowledge lookup.
- New endpoints: `GET /v1/gene/{id}/report`, `GET /v1/genes`, `POST /v1/geneset/summary`, `GET /v1/references`.

## Redesigned UI (the centerpiece)

Ground-up Streamlit rewrite with a custom theme and plain-English analysis throughout:

- **Gene explorer** — verdict hero (↑/↓/↔ + confidence), "What the data tells us" analysis, an aging-signal-by-data-type figure, cross-species panel, hallmarks, evidence with citations, curated DB flags, intervention bars, FAQs, references.
- **Aging clock** — PhenoAge scatter colored by age-acceleration, acceleration distribution, mortality-vs-age view, metric tiles, CSV upload + template.
- **Resilience** — rising variance and cross-correlation early-warning curves with plain-language limitations.
- Every figure has an exceptional caption.

## Docs & tests

- Rewrote `README.md`, the `DATA_SOURCES.md` honesty note, and the end-to-end notebook (executes cleanly).
- Updated the suite to assert the honest model: **79 tests pass**; `ruff`, `black`, and `mypy` are clean.

## Reviewer notes

- **One labeled simulation remains by necessity.** The clock and resilience tools need a per-subject biomarker matrix, and this environment blocks outbound biomedical APIs, so real NHANES rows couldn't be fetched. The bundled cohort is a transparent worked example of a *real* algorithm, badged `SIMULATED` in the UI, README, and About tab.
- Live upgrades are wired but dormant: `GEROQUERY_ALLOW_NETWORK=1` enables mygene.info resolution, and installing `pyaging`/`biolearn` auto-registers real DNA-methylation clocks.

items.title: fix(rust): canonical summation - full determinism + v10 re-baseline
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes issue #14's total-order panic and the deeper cross-process non-determinism it was a symptom of, in `pack_regions`' marginal-gain scoring (`roust-rs/src/core.rs`).

- **a4a29f6** — deterministic marginal keys: the true root cause of #14's panic was non-deterministic tie ordering when sorting candidates by marginal score (`f64` total-order comparator could observe two different orderings for equal/near-equal scores depending on HashMap iteration order feeding into the sort). Fixed by deriving a stable secondary sort key.
- **6a6c6a3** — canonical (sorted) summation order in `weight()`'s IDF accumulation: `f64` addition is not associative, so summing per-term IDF contributions in HashMap iteration order could produce different floating-point results (and therefore different marginal-gain rankings) across otherwise-identical runs. Fixed by summing in a canonical (sorted-key) order, closing the gap a4a29f6 alone didn't cover.

### Two-run identity proof

Two independent 300-instance runs at a4a29f6 (`/tmp/det_a.jsonl`, `/tmp/det_b.jsonl`) are **byte-identical** (md5 `2a909a46352abf1b2b72ddc090d6d0d1` both). A third run at the final commit (6a6c6a3, clean tree) — `lab/results_regions/full300_v10.jsonl` — matches both **content-identical** (only `engine_sha`/`engine_dirty` provenance fields differ, as expected across commits): 0/300 diffs once those two fields are excluded.

### Re-baseline (v4) vs v3

`lab/results_regions/agentless_metric_v4.json`, scored from v10 via a newly-parameterized copy of the metric script (`lab/agentless_metric_v4.py` — same scoring logic as v2/v3, `--predictions`/`--out` as CLI flags instead of hardcoded paths):

| metric | v3 | v4 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| FILE (277/300) | 92.33% | 92.33% | 0 |
| FUNCTION (exact, 123/300) | 41.0% | 41.0% | 0 |
| LINE all-or-nothing (107/300) | 35.67% | 35.67% | 0 |
| LINE mean-fraction covered | 0.4564 | 0.4564 | 0 |
| REGION PRECISION mean | 0.004486 | 0.004486 | 0 |

v4 is numerically **identical** to v3 field-for-field — this fix changes cross-process determinism guarantees, not scoring outcomes, on this baseline. FILE 277/300 sanity check holds. README's published FILE/FUNCTION/LINE/precision numbers (92.3/41.0/35.7/0.45%) are unchanged and need no update.

Refs #14, #4, #8.

## Summary

Optimizes the interactive `usage` and `analysis` dashboards so they stay usable when there are many models or the terminal is small. All changes are scoped to the TUI; static `--table`, `--text`, and `--json` output keep their exact, full-precision numbers.

## What changed

- **Scrollable, selectable model table.** The model list now scrolls instead of silently clipping the bottom rows. Navigate with the arrow keys, `PgUp`/`PgDn`, `g`/`G` (top/end), or `j`/`k`; the selected row is highlighted and a side scrollbar shows position. Navigation is keyboard-only, so the terminal's native drag-to-select and copy keep working.
- **Compact K/M/B number formatting (TUI only).** Long token / line / tool counts render as `1.23M`, `45.5B`, etc. instead of overflowing their columns. Costs stay precise and comma-grouped (`$13,489.34`). A single `format_compact` helper handles all of it; `format_number` still backs the static and machine-readable paths.
- **Reclaimed vertical space + graceful small-terminal handling.** The standalone title box (`Token Usage Statistics` / `Analysis Statistics`) is removed and the controls/star footer collapse to one line. On short windows the provider/quota band is dropped so the table keeps a usable height; below a hard minimum a centered "terminal too small" notice is shown instead of a broken layout.
- **Zero-usage models hidden.** Models with no tokens and no cost in the selected range are dropped from the table; the grand totals are unaffected.
- **Column rename.** `Cache Create` → `Cache Write` (parallel with `Cache Read`), applied to both the TUI and the static usage table for consistency.

## Shared refactor

Scroll state, the scrollable-table renderer, the adaptive layout, and the too-small guard live in `src/display/common/` so the two near-identical render frames share them instead of drifting.

## Testing

- `cargo test` (incl. new `format_compact` / `format_cost` unit + doc tests), `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `make fmt`, `uvx pre-commit run -a` — all green.
- pty smoke harness drives both dashboards through navigation keys and a tiny window (too-small guard), verifying clean exit, a restored terminal, and correct rendering.

items.title: docs: correct five README claims that no longer match what ships

labels.name: documentation
labels.description: Improvements or additions to documentation

items.body:
Audit of every factual claim in `README.md` against the source and against a
running install. Most of it held. Five things did not.

## The one a user actually hits

The Controls section opened with `scripts/pet.sh status`. That path only
resolves inside a git checkout — and the Install section three headings above
tells the reader to install the plugin, which gives them no checkout at all.
Every line of that section failed with `No such file or directory` for anyone
following the README top to bottom.

It now resolves the script out of the installed plugin instead. Hardcoding the
installed path would not have worked either: `pet.sh` keeps its runtime home
outside the plugin directory precisely because that directory moves on every
update.

Verified end to end — the resolver finds the script and `status` runs.

## Binary size: bounded, not corrected

The binary was advertised as `~200KB` in four places (README badge,
`plugin.json`, `marketplace.json`, `AGENTS.md`). A fresh `swiftc -O` produces
283,560 bytes ≈ 277KB.

Correcting the figure would have left the actual defect in place: nothing keeps
an exact number true, it has to be hand-synced across four files, and it had
already been wrong for several releases. The claim it supports is a contrast
with Electron, and a contrast survives a bound — under half a megabyte against
150MB is still three orders of magnitude, and stays true through any plausible
growth of one Swift file.

The badge was the worst of the four: it looks like something CI measured, and
is a hand-typed string, so it lied with more authority than the prose did.

`AGENTS.md` drops the figure outright rather than bounding it. That file states
its own job as *what will waste your time if you assume it*, and no decision
anywhere in the repo turns on how large the binary is.

## Build time: same treatment

"About two seconds" for the first-launch build, in README and
`llms-install.md`. Measured at 4.09s on Apple silicon — but that figure is not
ours to promise either. Compiler version and hardware move it, and a reader on
slower hardware would read a slow build as a broken install. Both now say "a
few seconds", which carries the only thing the number was there to say: this is
a pause, not a download.

Numbers that describe the code keep their precision. The 30s empty-grace window
and the measured 220s permission window elsewhere in `AGENTS.md` are a constant
and a recorded observation — neither promises anything the environment can
falsify.

## Overclaim

"The status words follow your system language" — they are translated for
Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese and Japanese, and fall back to English
for every other locale.

## A correction to `AGENTS.md`

The `Mood changes` note added in #12 said the renderer folds `sessions/*`. It
also folds the global `state` file, as one more priority input with a shorter
TTL. The practical advice — do not measure moods by polling `state` — is
unchanged, but it stands on last-writer-wins semantics, not on the renderer
ignoring the file. As written it would send the next reader looking in the
wrong place, and it would also cast doubt on the README's `state` puppet-string
trick, which does work.

## Checked and found accurate

Mood table and triggers, the `waiting > error > done > running` fold, 20fps
poll, ~30s idle exit, per-mood TTLs, `osascript` notifications (hence the
Script Editor attribution note), suppression while Claude is frontmost, the
three right-click items, cursor-following eyes, hover startle, tap hop, drag
position persistence, bubble-collapse persistence, Reduce Motion, live
`pet.json` reload, `--export` / `--validate`, both bundled examples still
validating, `--export` still round-tripping, and the macOS-only guard.

Not verified: the `/plugin …` REPL slash-command forms, which cannot be run
from a shell. Their CLI counterparts exist with exactly the documented
subcommand names.

Docs only — no code, no behavior change.

items.title: Add exact rational arithmetic with ExactQuantity and Rational
items.body:
## Summary

This PR introduces exact arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic to effect-units, enabling lossless quantity calculations. The core addition is a new `Rational` type representing reduced fractions of bigints, paired with `ExactQuantity` — a quantity type parameterized by unit and backed by rationals instead of floats. All arithmetic operations are exact; division returns `Option` since ℚ has no infinities or NaN.

## Key Changes

- **`Rational` module** (`src/Rational.ts`): Arbitrary-precision rational numbers with field operations (sum, multiply, divide, negate, reciprocal), comparisons, and conversions to/from floats and BigDecimal. Every rational is stored in reduced form with sign normalized to the numerator.

- **`ExactQuantity` module** (`src/ExactQuantity.ts`): Exact quantities tagged with a unit tree, supporting arithmetic (`sum`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, `times`, `over`) and comparisons. Includes Schema codecs for wire serialization in canonical rational form (`"3/2"`, `"-3/2"`, `"3"`).

- **`ExactTemperature` module** (`src/ExactTemperature.ts`): Absolute temperature as a rational in kelvins (not an `ExactQuantity`, since adding two absolute temperatures is nonsensical). Supports conversions between Kelvin, Celsius, and Fahrenheit scales exactly.

- **Exact unit modules**: `ExactLength`, `ExactArea`, `ExactVolume`, `ExactMass`, `ExactDuration`, `ExactSpeed`, `ExactAcceleration`, `ExactForce`, `ExactEnergy`, `ExactPower`, `ExactPressure`, `ExactDensity`, `ExactTorque`, `ExactCharge`, `ExactCurrent`, `ExactVoltage`, `ExactResistance`, `ExactCapacitance`, `ExactInductance`, `ExactMolarity`, `ExactSubstanceAmount`, `ExactIlluminance`, `ExactLuminousIntensity`, `ExactLuminousFlux`, `ExactLuminance`, `ExactPixels` — each wrapping `ExactQuantity` with unit-specific constructors and extractors.

- **`Unit.custom()`** (`src/Unit.ts`): New `Custom<Id>` unit type for user-defined base units, composing freely with `Product` and `Rate`. Enables consumer-authored modules like Money without modifying the library.

- **Exact prefix and constants** (`src/internal/exactPrefix.ts`, `src/internal/exactConstants.ts`): Rational counterparts of SI prefixes and shared conversion factors, ensuring prefix math is exact (all powers of ten).

- **Comprehensive test suite**: Property-based tests for Rational field laws, ExactQuantity arithmetic, roundtrip conversions, and exact constant pinning. Includes test utilities (`test/exactTestUtils.ts`) for shared test patterns.

- **README updates**: Documents the new Exact* modules and their role in the library.

## Notable Implementation Details

- Rationals are immutable value objects with `Equal` and `Hash` support; equivalent fractions (e.g., 2/4 and 1/2) are one value.
- `ExactQuantity` arithmetic is closed except for division, which returns `Option` to handle potential zero divisors.
- Temperature conversions (Celsius ↔ Fahrenheit ↔ Kelvin) are exact via rational arithmetic, avoiding float rounding.
- All conversion factors in exact modules are derived from exact rational sources (SI definitions, 1959 yard/pound agreement).
- Wire format for `ExactQuantity` uses canonical rational encoding with no precision ceiling, enabling lossless serialization.

items.title: Refresh six-run CLAS benchmark after hold-continuation carve-out (#349)
items.body:
## Summary

Docs-only refresh of the six-run PPC moving CLAS benchmark, regenerated from the merged develop tip (c93c1d0 = #349 hold-continuation carve-out). The develop-tip rebuild was byte-checked against the validated v3 outputs (nagoya_run2 md5 `865c46a9398bb65a782cb0f33c5c69ea`, identical), so the published FIX counts/rates are exactly the reviewed #349 validation results.

A follow-up commit on this branch (`aae7234`) fixes a scoring-methodology bug found while reviewing this refresh: see "Methodology fix" below. It changes the precision numbers (FIX RMS2D etc.) but not the FIX counts/rates from the table above.

## Per-run results (libgnss++ FIX / FIX RMS2D, vs prior)

| Run | FIX | prior | FIX RMS2D | prior | >3 m FIX |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Tokyo 1 | 9.735% | 9.702% | 0.452 m | 0.453 m | 0 |
| Tokyo 2 | 20.891% | 19.219% | 0.381 m | 0.387 m | 0 |
| Tokyo 3 | 37.623% | 37.387% | 0.327 m | 0.327 m | 0 |
| Nagoya 1 | 36.724% | 36.605% | 0.889 m | 0.888 m | 0 |
| Nagoya 2 | 23.863% | 23.117% | 0.787 m | 0.783 m | 0 |
| Nagoya 3 | 4.865% | 4.865% | 0.959 m | 0.959 m | 0 |

**Aggregate: 23.645% / 0.593 m → 24.110% / 0.592 m**, 14,046 FIX epochs over 58,258 scored. FIX counts, fix%, and coverage above are unchanged by the methodology fix below — only the RMS2D/precision columns move (see the corrected table).

## Changes

- Regenerated `docs/ppc_clas_full_{metrics.json,table.md,comparison.png,trajectories.png,errors.png}` via `scripts/generate_ppc_clas_full_comparison.py` (min-epoch-coverage 0.92)
- Synced the README condensed table, benchmark-summary row, and FIX-epoch prose
- Updated `docs/ppc_clas_validation.md` "Current verdict" (#349 numbers, Nagoya 2 now above target)
- **Follow-up (`aae7234`)**: scoring methodology fix — see below. Touches `scripts/generate_ppc_clas_full_comparison.py`, `scripts/generate_ppc_clas_scorecard.py`, `tests/test_ppc_clas_scorecard.py`, and all four doc/data files above, plus `README.md` and `docs/ppc_clas_validation.md`.

## Methodology fix: drop the lever-arm double-correction

While reviewing this refresh, we found that CLAS scoring applied an IMU→antenna lever-arm correction to the reference (`apply_lever_arm=True`) on top of a PPC `reference.csv` that is **already antenna-positioned** — a double correction.

Decisive evidence: projecting no-lever-arm fixed-epoch error vectors into the vehicle body frame (via reference heading) on Nagoya run3 gives a mean of **(0.075, 0.088) m ≈ zero**, not the **(0.593, -0.670) m** horizontal lever offset that would appear if the reference were truly at the IMU. A per-epoch error correlation of **r=0.991** between our solver and a real MRTKLIB v0.5.1 rerun, on 206 co-fixed Nagoya run3 epochs, confirms the bias is common-mode and reference-side, not solver-side. The old double-correction inflated FIX RMS2D by roughly **0.89 m (Nagoya) / 0.31 m (Tokyo)**. The published MRTKLIB v0.4.2 targets were computed without any lever-arm transform (raw reference), so the raw-reference basis is the apples-to-apples one — and it's what this PR now uses by default.

`scripts/generate_ppc_clas_full_comparison.py` and `scripts/generate_ppc_clas_scorecard.py` now default to `apply_lever_arm=False` for CLAS scoring; the lever-arm path is kept behind an explicit `--apply-lever-arm` opt-in flag for reproducing historical numbers. No non-CLAS script was touched.

### Corrected six-run table (raw-reference basis, same convention as MRTKLIB)

| Run | libgnss++ FIX RMS2D | MRTKLIB FIX RMS2D | >3 m FIX |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tokyo 1 | **0.306 m** | 0.747 m | 0 |
| Tokyo 2 | **0.326 m** | 0.514 m | 0 |
| Tokyo 3 | **0.185 m** | 0.801 m | 0 |
| Nagoya 1 | **0.444 m** | 1.105 m | 0 |
| Nagoya 2 | **0.614 m** | 1.119 m | 19 |
| Nagoya 3 | **0.317 m** | 0.318 m | 0 |
| **Aggregate** | **0.370 m** | — | **19** |

libgnss++ FIX RMS2D is now lower than the published MRTKLIB v0.4.2 value on **all six runs**. FIX counts, fix%, and `fixed_over_3m`-per-run selection logic are byte-identical to the table above — only the reference point used for scoring changed.

### Newly visible >3 m tail (not a regression)

Removing the lever-arm bias exposes 19 FIX epochs (0.03% of 58,258 scored) with horizontal error above 3 m, all in a single contiguous **4-second burst on Nagoya 2** (TOW 556406.4–556410.4, errors 3.17–3.20 m, max 3.200 m), inside the known seed-geometry `maxdiffp` reset zone. We independently verified this is **pre-existing, not introduced by #349**: the identical 19 epochs (same TOWs, same errors to 0.01 m) are present in the pre-#349 baseline pos file (`clas_current_develop_20260723/nagoya_run2.pos`). Under the old lever-arm scoring this burst sat at ~2.4–2.5 m (old Nagoya 2 max was 2.486 m), so the previous "0 FIX epochs above 3 m" claim was itself partly a flattering scoring artifact. The other five runs still have zero FIX epochs above 3 m. Fixing this burst is tracked as a follow-up (`docs/ppc_clas_validation.md` next-gates item 2).

No code changes to the solver itself in this PR — this is scoring/docs only.

## Summary

Adds a new paper, **The Workspace Is the Self-Improving Agent**, and groups the existing design essays under a new `docs/papers/` folder.

The paper synthesizes the two companion essays into a single thesis: because the workspace holds *code* (roles, collection schemas, skills, automations) and not just data, **the workspace is the agent** — and an agent that authors its own workspace is **self-improving**. A collection skill is therefore a real application the agent builds *into itself*, dissolving the app/agent and build/run boundaries.

Intellectual lineage is anchored to **Karpathy's *LLM Knowledge Bases*** idea (the self-maintained wiki), extended from self-maintained *memory* to self-maintained *applications*. *The Log is the Agent* (arXiv:2605.21997) is a brief contrast note only.

items.title: docs: explain JSON integer precision loss in --format=json and how to read it correctly
items.body:
This pull request improves documentation and developer guidance around handling large integer fields in CCIP JSON output, especially for JavaScript/TypeScript users. It adds a new SDK guide, enhances CLI documentation, and clarifies best practices for parsing JSON with large integers, to prevent silent precision loss in JavaScript and other languages with limited integer precision.

**Documentation improvements for JSON integer precision:**

* Added a new guide, `json-integer-precision`, to the SDK docs explaining why fields like `chainSelector`, token amounts, and fees are emitted as plain JSON numbers, the risks of using `JSON.parse` in JavaScript, and how to use `jsonParse` from `@chainlink/ccip-sdk` to safely handle large integers. The guide also covers handling in Python, Go, Postgres, and jq.
* Included the new guide in the SDK documentation sidebar for easier discovery.

**CLI documentation updates:**

* Updated the CLI README to clarify that `--format=json` emits large integers as plain JSON numbers, not quoted strings, and warns users about precision loss when using `JSON.parse`, `jq`, or other parsers.
* Added a new "Scripting & Automation" section to the CLI README, providing concrete examples of the precision issue, correct parsing strategies in various languages, and a reference to the new SDK guide.

**Code comments for agent developers:**

* Improved comments in `ccip-cli/src/index.ts` to explicitly warn that agents should use `jsonParse` instead of `JSON.parse` when consuming CLI JSON output, due to the risk of integer corruption above 2^53.

items.title: fix: align MySQL and MSSQL codegen type maps with driver defaults
items.body:
## Problem (#68)

Generated schema types must match what the driver actually returns — that is the library's core promise. Two mismatches:

1. **MySQL `bigint` mapped to `string`**, but mysql2 returns BIGINT as a JS **number** unless `supportBigNumbers`/`bigNumberStrings` is enabled — which neither the adapter nor the CLI configures. The extremely common `BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT` PK was typed `string` while runtime values are numbers: `row.id.padStart(...)` typechecked and crashed.
2. **MSSQL `decimal`/`numeric`/`money`/`smallmoney` mapped to `string`**, but tedious parses these into JS numbers by default (with precision loss beyond 2^53). `bigint` → `string` there was already correct.

The pg map (int8/numeric/money → `string`) matches pg-types defaults and is untouched.

## Fix

- `mysql.ts`: `bigint` → `number` (`decimal`/`numeric` stay `string` — mysql2 does return those as strings).
- `mssql.ts`: `decimal`/`numeric`/`money`/`smallmoney` → `number` (`bigint` stays `string`).
- README's "conservative on purpose" paragraph replaced with a per-driver statement of actual defaults, including the flags that change them.

## Tests

Type-map locks updated to the driver-default expectations (including `smallmoney`); mocked MySQL introspection test updated. Full suite passes.

Closes #68

items.title: communication: add writing-for-readers skill
items.body:
Problem: Andrey's rules for published prose (articles, blog posts, course lessons, landing page copy) only existed as the accept/reject history of one live rewrite, so every new piece re-derived them by hand. The two skills already in `skills/communication/` cover the other two audiences: `agent-to-human` for what an agent hands back to a person, `human-to-agent` for instructions a human writes for an agent. Nothing covered prose a reader finds on their own.

Solution: New `skills/communication/writing-for-readers/SKILL.md`, 167 lines.

- Voice and length first: explain it out loud to a colleague; assume the first draft is twice as long as it needs to be. The reference rewrite went 350 words to 155 with no fact lost.
- Nine named tells, each with the rejected text and the approved replacement: aphorism pair, clipped callback, thesis opener, negate-then-correct, announcing the structure, speech close, em dashes, unused precision, avoidable jargon.
- A Keep section: numbers that carry the argument, source links on their phrase, second person, the technical claim unchanged.
- A five-step mechanical pass over a finished draft, ending on first-sentence and last-sentence checks.

Every example is the real before/after of the "Connections multiply with every parallel session" section, pulled from the brief of the sibling My Website task "Rewrite course and lesson copy in the human voice" rather than invented.

Name: `writing-for-readers`, not the suggested `content-writing`. It names the audience the way its two siblings do, and "content" would not tell a loading agent that this is the published-prose skill and `agent-to-human` is the reply skill.

Overlap with `agent-to-human` is handled by reference, not restatement: the jargon tell points at that skill for the general plain-words discipline, and the `description` ends by sending chat replies, status updates and PR bodies there.

Also: registered in the `Communication` group in `skills.sh.json` with the group description widened to three audiences, and a row added to the README table.

Testing: `bun test` — 19 pass, 0 fail, including the guard that every skill directory has a `SKILL.md`.

items.title: GROOT N1.7 update: Thor NVFP4 + FA4 performance tier
items.body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in NVFP4 + FA4 performance tier for GROOT N1.7 on Jetson AGX Thor (SM110). The default FP8 path is unchanged.

Measured on the `GR00T-N1.7` LIBERO fine-tune (`libero_10`), one camera, 4 denoising steps, batch 1, medians over 20 iterations after 5 warmup iterations, on a fixture captured from a real `libero_10` observation through the official preprocessing path (JetPack 7.2, MAXN):

| Tier | Backbone | Action head | E2E | Frequency |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FP8 (default, unchanged) | 11.0 ms | 25.8 ms | 36.8 ms | 27.2 Hz |
| NVFP4 + FA4 (`use_fp4=True`) | 8.4 ms | 15.2 ms | **23.7 ms** | **42.3 Hz** |

Run as one same-session A/B/A: FP8 36.76 ms → NVFP4 23.65 ms → FP8 36.85 ms. Action cosine between the tiers on that fixture is **1.000000**.

On the base `GR00T-N1.7-3B` checkpoint with a 2-view fixture (`T=40`, same protocol): FP8 50.2 ms (20 Hz) → NVFP4 29.9 ms (33 Hz), also A/B/A (51.6 / 29.9 / 50.2), action cosine 0.99994.

CUDA-graph replays on the new tier are bit-identical (the masked-softmax attention also removes a long-standing source of replay nondeterminism in the FP8 tier's logits padding). On an 8-sample aux set captured from the base checkpoint, 7 of 8 samples hold action cosine >= 0.9993 against the FP8 tier with a worst sample of 0.9976 — deployments that are accuracy-critical should validate on the target task rather than on cosine alone, or stay on the FP8 tier.

An earlier revision of this branch carried a `dit_fp8_layers` precision ladder. It was removed before review: with every DiT layer marked for FP8 the captured graph still produced the all-NVFP4 result, so the option did not do what it documented. The last commit removes the knob, its per-layer gate, and the benchmark flag rather than shipping unverified behavior.

## What is in the tier

- **NVFP4 DiT action head** — every DiT GEMM (fused self-attn QKV, cross-attn Q, attention output, both FFN projections) runs as a block-scaled NVFP4 GEMM with fused bf16 bias / bias+residual / bias+tanh-GELU+FP4-output epilogues. At M=41 the DiT is weight-bandwidth-bound, so halving weight bytes is the dominant win. Activation quantization is dynamic per-16-element (no calibration pass).
- **NVFP4 cross-KV projections** — the 32 per-frame K/V GEMMs quarter their weight traffic.
- **Fused norm→FP4 / norm→FP8 front-ends** — AdaLN and the pre-FFN LayerNorm emit FP4 directly (bit-identical to the two-step chain); the ViT / VL-self-attn LayerNorms emit FP8 directly, dropping the fp16 intermediate's write and read-back.
- **Vectorized backbone small kernels** — 16-byte-load rewrites of the per-head RMSNorms, LayerNorms, static FP8 quantize, split-half RoPE, GQA head expand, and residual add. The scalar originals issue 2–4 B accesses and sit far under the LPDDR5X floor. Element math matches; RoPE / quantize / head-expand / residual are bit-exact.
- **Masked-softmax MHA** — the softmax touches only the valid `S_kv` columns, so the per-layer full-buffer `-inf` logits pre-fill disappears; the DiT self-attention also reads the fused QKV GEMM output in place (token stride 3D), dropping three split copies per layer.
- **FA4 attention** — the three backbone MHA sites (ViT multi-view, LLM causal GQA with `pack_gqa`, VL-self-attn) run the vendored FlashAttention-4 (CuTe-DSL) forward, falling back to the existing fmha/cuBLAS chain when the `thor-fa4` runtime deps are absent.

## Shared-code changes

Only two files outside `groot_n17` carry behavior:

- `flash_rt/api.py` — `use_fp4=True` with `config="groot_n17"` on Thor routes to the new frontend and falls back to the FP8 tier when `flash_rt_fp4` is unavailable. Pi0.5's `use_fp4` routing is untouched.
- `flash_rt/hardware/thor/fa4_backend.py` — the Thor chip string now follows the installed `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` (4.4.x only accepts `sm_110a`; 4.5+ needs the `sm_101a` alias). Previously the loader always requested `sm_101a`, so on 4.4.x FA4 failed to compile and every caller silently fell back to fmha. Call sites: LingBot (`flash_rt/models/lingbot/kernel_ops.py`) and Cosmos3-Edge (`flash_rt/models/cosmos3_edge/layer_ref.py`) — both keep their existing behavior on 4.5+ and now get the working FA4 path on 4.4.x.

The shared build surface also changes, in gated form: two new compilation units (`csrc/kernels/attention_mha_masked.cu`, `csrc/kernels/vec_fp16_backbone.cu`) join `flash_rt_kernels`, but only on SM100-class builds — CMake adds them under `ENABLE_SM100_CUTLASS` and defines `FLASHRT_HAVE_THOR_VLA_KERNELS`, and their bindings in `csrc/bindings.cpp` are guarded by the same define, so source and binding drop together on SM8x. The NVFP4 frontend probes for those bindings up front and fails naming the build flag rather than dying inside graph capture.

Everything else is additive: new `csrc` kernels with new symbols, a new frontend subclass, and gated branches in the N1.7 pipeline.

## Tests

`tests/test_groot_n17_thor_fp4_kernels.py` — 16 contracts covering the NVFP4 GEMM epilogues against a torch reference, the bf16 activation quantizer, the fused DiT norms (bit-exact vs the two-step chain), the vectorized backbone helpers, and masked-softmax MHA against the pre-filled variant with a poisoned logits scratch. The masked softmax is additionally pinned at `S_kv` = 1024 / 1025 / 2048 in both dtypes against torch SDPA, since 1024 is where its register-tiled path hands over to the multi-pass one. Skips cleanly without CUDA or the optional `flash_rt_fp4` extension.

`tests/test_groot_n17_thor_fp4_routing.py` — 5 contracts on the public `load_model` behavior the tier adds: `use_fp4=True` selects the NVFP4 frontend, a missing or NVFP4-less `flash_rt_fp4` falls back to FP8, `use_fp4` with `use_fp16` is rejected, and the default route is unchanged. Frontends are stubbed, so these need no GPU or checkpoint.

Regression run on Thor (`tests/test_groot_n17_*`, `test_thor_groot_attn_backend`, `test_build_inventory`, `test_load_model_use_fp8_kwarg`): 156 passed, 36 skipped, 1 pre-existing environment failure (`test_e2e_action_cosines_with_hf_noise` needs a newer `transformers` for `denormalize_action`; it fails the same way on `main`).

## Reproduce

The A/B/A above is three runs of the same command with the tier flipped;
`--ref-out` / `--ref-in` carry the FP8 output forward so the FP4 run reports
the cross-tier action cosine, and `--min-cosine` turns it into a gate:

```bash
# A: FP8 tier, save its actions as the precision reference
python benchmarks/groot_n17_thor_latency.py \
    --ckpt <n17-libero-checkpoint-dir> --aux <1-camera-aux-fixture.pt> \
    --tier fp8 --views 1 --embodiment libero_sim \
    --warmup 5 --iters 20 --ref-out fp8_actions.pt

# B: NVFP4 tier, compared against it (exits non-zero below the threshold)
python benchmarks/groot_n17_thor_latency.py \
    --ckpt <n17-libero-checkpoint-dir> --aux <1-camera-aux-fixture.pt> \
    --tier fp4 --views 1 --embodiment libero_sim \
    --warmup 5 --iters 20 --ref-in fp8_actions.pt --min-cosine 0.999

# A': FP8 again, to show the pair is not regime drift
python benchmarks/groot_n17_thor_latency.py \
    --ckpt <n17-libero-checkpoint-dir> --aux <1-camera-aux-fixture.pt> \
    --tier fp8 --views 1 --embodiment libero_sim --warmup 5 --iters 20
```

`tests/_helpers/groot_n17/capture_aux_multi.py --views N` captures a fixture with a restricted camera count, which is how the one-camera fixture above was produced.

## Base

Rebased onto current `main` (after #159 / #160 / #161). The overlap with those is docs and registration only — `README.md`, `docs/stable_api.md`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `flash_rt/api.py` — and the rebase was clean. #160's RTX backbone-graph work is untouched; this PR only refreshes the GROOT N1.7 benchmark table's RTX 5090 row to the 16.61 ms full-graph number that #160 produced, since that table still carried the pre-graph 22 ms.

## Docs

`README.md`, `USAGE.md`, `docs/stable_api.md`, and `docs/benchmark_comparison.md` record the tier, its flag, the precision ladder, and the measured numbers with the harness definition. `docs/benchmark_comparison.md` also carries NVIDIA's published TensorRT reference table for the same model family on the same board, alongside the camera-count-matched FlashRT rows and the 2-view base-checkpoint rows, each with its harness stated.

## Background

P0–P6 are complete (PR #11–#14 merged). The 147 passing tests are
overwhelmingly happy-path and single-point-race coverage — there is
**no test that proves the system stays safe under partition, crash, and
recovery combinations.** We believe election safety, state-machine
safety, committed-entry durability, and 2PC atomicity all hold, but we
cannot currently demonstrate any of them.

P7 closes that gap: it moves the project from "wrote a Raft" to "can
take responsibility for its correctness."

## Changes (docs-only)

- **ROADMAP.md**: P6 marked complete in the phase table; full P7 section
  added — problem statement, goal, approach (virtual clock + network,
  fault injection, invariant checker, sequential reference model,
  seed-driven fuzzing), non-goals, acceptance criteria, planned work
  (described by capability, not pinned to PR numbers), and open
  questions.
- **README.md**: current phase → P7; phase table updated; candidate list
  notes DST as active.
- **CHANGELOG.md**: records the roadmap decision.

## Planned work (described by capability, not PR numbers)

How this splits into PRs is decided as the work lands — GitHub assigns
numbers at creation, so pinning them would be false precision.

- Abstract transport + clock behind traits (`real` impls, no behavior
  change) — the foundation.
- Deterministic virtual clock + network + fault scheduler + seed driver.
- Safety invariants + sequential reference model.
- Crash / restart / partition / heal scenarios + seed fuzzing + shrinker
  + CI + docs.

## Notes

- No code or test changes in this PR; it only pins the direction.
- Open questions (clock abstraction depth, message- vs byte-level
  simulation, CI seed budget) are listed in ROADMAP.md to resolve as
  work starts.

items.title: fix(playground): preserve bigint precision and avoid stale statement cache
items.body:
## Summary

Two independent fixes to the SQL Playground sandbox executor, both found while
building the frontend against a running API.

**Prepared-statement cache (`26000`).** The sandbox runs `DISCARD ALL` after
each query to clear session-scoped state (advisory locks, etc.). `DISCARD ALL`
deallocates prepared statements, but pgx's default exec mode caches them by
name, so the next query on the same pooled connection reused a statement the
server had already dropped and failed with `prepared statement "stmtcache_..."
does not exist`. Fixed by running every sandbox statement in
`pgx.QueryExecModeExec` (no named-statement cache, binary decoding preserved).
Caching buys the sandbox nothing since each user query is one-off. Reproduced
first (same query, single-connection pool, failed on the 2nd run), then fixed;
a regression test covers it.

**bigint precision.** `int64`/`uint64` were passed through as JSON numbers, so
values above `2^53` lost precision in the browser. They are now rendered as
strings, consistent with how numerics and timestamps are already returned;
smaller integers still pass through as JSON numbers.

## Type of change

- [x] fix: bug fix

## Roadmap phase

Phase 2 - SQL Playground (fixes to the already-merged sandbox).

## How was this tested?

- [x] `go test ./...` passes locally against real PostgreSQL, including the new
  regression test and an extended typed-columns test asserting `2^53 + 1` is
  returned as an exact string.
- End to end against the running API: four sequential identical queries all
  return `200` (previously the 2nd failed with `26000`), and
  `SELECT 9007199254740993::bigint` returns the exact string `"9007199254740993"`.

## Database and migrations

- Delete this whole section if the PR does not touch the schema or queries.

## Checklist

- [x] Title follows Conventional Commits
- [x] Self-reviewed the diff
- [ ] Docs updated (README): n/a (no behavior change to document)
- [ ] CI is green (pending)

items.title: Build the application against the spec
items.body:
The README has been the specification since the map closed. This is the first code written against it — every rule was already decided, and where the spec was ambiguous the reading taken is commented at the site with its section number.

## What is here

Every route in §1.5's closed URL set, the compute engine of §8, the schema of §2.10 reproduced line by line, and the two payload contracts at v4 and v2.

The compute engine is the part that could not have been re-derived from documentation. The parser maps every field by name from each table's own `%F` line, because a positional read returns correct data from a 6.0 export and silently wrong data from an 8.3 one. The calendar decoder implements the shapes ticket 051 recorded as undecodable and the end-of-day rule ticket 052 specified — neither of which `tools/fixture-gen` has. The tracer walks the driving path as a **set** rather than a chain, so a tie keeps every branch.

## What holds it

The committed corpus. 29 fixtures, each carrying a golden written from what the generator *intended* to emit rather than from what any parser reports.

The tracer matches the `as_read_from_the_file` block on all 28 walkable files and reproduces the corpus README's pooled figures to the activity — **97.0% recall at 97.9% precision** — with the four documented disagreements asserted as hard numbers, so an unexplained *improvement* fails the suite too.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `biome ci .` | clean |
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| `vitest run` | **1,134 passing** |
| `measure.mjs --verify` | **29/29** |
| `next build` | green with no database and no Clerk keys |

Measured on generated programmes: 6,100 activities parse→derive in 496 ms, and `derived.json` holds at **22.7 KB for 20,000 activities** against the 150 KB ceiling — 10× the activities costs 2 KB.

## Defects the review caught, since fixed

- **`Content-Encoding` was signed but not allowed at preflight.** It is not a CORS-safelisted request header, so every presigned PUT would have been denied and upload could never have worked. §10.4 and §5.6 genuinely disagree here; §10.4 wins, and the `edge-contract` job derives its preflight list from the presign's own output so the two cannot drift apart again.
- **The true race of §5.8 was classified as transient.** A content-hash collision surfacing on the publish `UPDATE` burnt three sweep retries and reported an internal error instead of the offer to fork.
- **Size bands put a 2,000-activity programme in `m`.** §1.5 names 2,000 in both bands; the partition that makes all four disjoint puts each shared boundary in the upper one.
- **Middleware ran on Edge by omission**, against §10.2's *"Node.js, not Edge, everywhere"*.

## Not verified

**No statement has ever been executed against a live Postgres or MinIO** — Docker was unavailable in the session that built this. Every query typechecks and the SQL reads correctly, but the CI stack job on this PR is the first real run. The three things I would watch are the generated `search_tsv` expression, the partial-index predicate, and `db.batch`.

## Not built

The production-edge canary (§10.5) and the live `robots.txt` monitor, both of which assert things that do not exist until the estate is provisioned by 026. Recorded in `docs/build-backlog.md` §D alongside the tidies the review found and I did not take.

items.title: feat!: modernize toolchain and dependencies (P0)
items.body:
Implements **P0** from the production-readiness review: make the project compile and build again on a current toolchain.

## Changes

- **Dependencies**: `gmod` 10.2.2 → 17.0.1, `sysinfo` 0.22.4 → 0.39.6 (real version requirements, no more `\"*\"`). This drops the `ntapi 0.3.6` transitive that fails with hard error E0793 on any rustc since mid-2023 — the reason the locked tree stopped compiling. `lazy_static` is gone entirely, replaced by `std::sync::LazyLock`; sysinfo is built with `default-features = false, features = [\"system\"]`, which also sheds the rayon subtree.
- **Toolchain**: pinned `nightly-2026-08-01` (gmod-rs still requires nightly) with rustfmt/clippy components and all four release targets declared, so local and CI toolchains match. `#![feature(c_unwind)]` removed — stabilized since Rust 1.71.
- **Units/precision fix**: `get_memory()`/`get_swap()` now push Lua numbers (f64) in **bytes**. The old path cast through pointer-width `LuaInt`, which is i32 on the 32-bit builds and would overflow at 2 GiB the moment units became bytes. Doubles are integer-exact to 8 PiB. README updated accordingly.
- **Bug fixes**: `get_host_name` error no longer says "system version"; removed the leftover `"Goodbye from binary module!"` print on unload.
- **New in gmod 17**: client (`gmcl`) builds now call `restore_stdout()` on unload — required by gmod 17's stdout override, which otherwise crashes the game when the module unloads. The `gmcl` crate feature now properly forwards to `gmod/gmcl` so server builds don't compile the client machinery at all.
- **Hygiene**: error helper returns `!` to match `lua_error` semantics (call sites no longer read as fall-through bugs); dead `err!` macro arms removed; release profile added (`lto`, `codegen-units = 1`, `strip = \"symbols\"` — replaces the CI strip step); Cargo.toml gains description/license/repository metadata and `publish = false`.

## Breaking change

`get_memory()` and `get_swap()` return **bytes** (previously KiB). Conventional-commit footer is present so the release tooling bumps major (v2.0.0).

## Verification

- `cargo check` on all four targets (win32/win64/linux32/linux64), both realms (`sv` and `cl`/`--features gmcl`): clean
- `cargo clippy --all-targets` both realms: no warnings
- `cargo fmt --check`: clean
- `cargo build --release` both realms on win64: links, 205 KB stripped DLL

## Notes

- CI on this PR will fail — the existing workflow is still the broken pre-P1 pipeline (archived actions-rs, `::set-output`). P1 replaces it; this PR deliberately changes no workflows.
- Not runtime-tested in a live Garry's Mod instance yet; the GluaTest job planned for P1 covers that.

items.title: Q1.23 fixed-point quantization study (#4)
items.body:
## Summary

Closes #4. Quantifies the error introduced by running the reference model in the signed **Q1.23** saturating datapath the RTL will use (README §4), versus the floating-point golden reference (`Mesh2D`).

> **Stacked on #36.** Base is `3-cfl-stability-study` because this work builds on the MATLAB `Mesh2D` introduced there. GitHub will auto-retarget this PR to `main` once #36 merges.

## What's added

- **`model/QMesh2D.m`** — bit-faithful Q1.23 fixed-point mesh: integer `Q.frac` state, `Q2.46` multiply → round/`>>23`, 48-bit guard accumulator, saturation on store. Configurable `frac` / `coeff_frac` / `rounding` to drive the sweeps.
- **`model/quantization_study.m`** — float vs Q1.23 SNR, noise floor, decay-time drift; coefficient-precision sweep; round-vs-truncate; accumulator guard budget; prints M1 recommendations.
- **`docs/fixed_point_analysis.md`** — written error budget + recommendations carried into M1 (`fdtd_pkg`).
- Doc/milestone updates (`model/README.md`, `docs/README.md`, `MILESTONES.md`).

## Findings

Reference operating point: 32×32 fixed boundary, `fs=48k`, `c=144`, `sigma=1.5`, 0.8 s, strike scaled for head-room.

| Metric | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Q1.23 SNR vs float | **66.6 dB**, −85.6 dBFS noise floor, **0 saturations** |
| Decay-time drift (T60) | **+0.05 %** (4.61 s vs 4.61 s) |
| Coefficient cliff | below ~14–15 bits `sigk1 → 1.0`, damping vanishes, T60 → 500–1400 s |
| Rounding vs truncation | truncation adds +4.2e-5 DC bias (vs 4.7e-8) the recursion integrates |
| Accumulator guard | 48-bit @ Q.23 = 25 integer bits, ample; strike-to-peak gain ~5.4× |

Headline result: **coefficient precision, not state width, is the dominant risk** — `a0`/`sigk1 = 1 − σk ≈ 1 − 2⁻¹⁵`, so the damping lives in the low bits. Recommendation: carry `a0`/`sigk1` at full Q1.23 width, round-to-nearest on every `>>23`, keep the 48-bit guard accumulator and saturate only on store, and scale the excitation input for head-room.

## Testing

Verified in GNU Octave: `QMesh2D` reproduces the float reference at high precision and gives the SNR/decay numbers above. Plotting is standard MATLAB, guarded to skip gracefully in headless environments. The GHDL CI (`make -C sim`) is unaffected by this MATLAB-only change.

items.title: Bump meshoptimizer from 1.1.1 to 1.2.0

labels.name: dependencies
labels.description: Pull requests that update a dependency file

labels.name: javascript
labels.description: Pull requests that update javascript code

items.body:
Bumps [meshoptimizer](https://github.com/zeux/meshoptimizer) from 1.1.1 to 1.2.0.
Release notes

Sourced from meshoptimizer's releases.

v1.2

This release introduces a major new feature, tangent frame generation, significantly improves vertex decoding performance on Intel/AMD CPUs and also adds several smaller features and improvements. Highlights:

A new tangent frame generator can generate tangents from either indexed or unindexed triangle mesh with positions/normals/texture coordinates. The generator implements MikkTSpace algorithm, but is significantly faster to run (~6-10x faster than mikktspace.c depending on the input structure). Note that the generation result is a per-corner tangent and applying the tangents to the indexed mesh may require splitting source vertices; consult documentation for details. By default, the algorithm uses a modified weighting scheme that significantly improves tangent quality around beveled regions in the mesh, with meshopt_TangentCompatible option provided for cases where exact compatibility with mikktspace.c is important (e.g. normal map baking workflows).

Vertex decoding (meshopt_decodeVertexBuffer) implementation for Intel/AMD CPUs has been significantly revised. The new mostly branchless SSSE3 implementation is usually ~20-45% faster than it was in previous releases, with the gains depending on CPU and the data composition; it's typical to see gains in the upper half of this range for engine-packed data. This implementation is automatically selected on compatible CPUs (SSSE3+POPCNT), with no change in data encoding, so to get this performance boost a library update is sufficient. If the code is compiled with AVX-512/AVX10 support (which is currently only selected at compile time when opted into), the decoding is an additional ~10% faster.

Additionally, new index filtering functions are provided to remove degenerate/duplicate triangles based on positional identity, which can be especially helpful for raytracing performance, a function for computing optimal shared exponent for cluster positions can be used to prepare geometry for upcoming DXR2 Compressed1 format, and clusterlod.h now implements DAG BVH construction via clodBuildHierarchy.

The majority of the work on the core library in this release has been sponsored by Valve; thank you!

Library improvements

  • New experimental function for generating tangents based on MikkTSpace algorithm, meshopt_generateTangents
  • New experimental functions for filtering out degenerate and duplicate triangles based on positional identity, meshopt_filterIndexBuffer/meshopt_filterIndexBufferMulti
  • New experimental function for computing optimal shared exponent for cluster positions which can be used with upcoming DXR2 Compressed1 format
  • meshopt_encode/decodeMeshlet* functions, meshopt_extractMeshletIndices and meshopt_optimizeMeshletLevel functions, as well as meshopt_SimplifyVertex_Priority and meshopt_SimplifyRegularizeLight flags, are now stable.
  • Significantly improve meshopt_decodeVertexBuffer performance on existing data for Intel/AMD CPUs (20-45% faster depending on CPU and data characteristics)
  • Significantly improve performance of meshopt_partitionClusters on larger partition sizes (~2x for target_size 64, ~200x for 1024)
  • Improve post-compression ratio for meshlets encoded using meshlet codec after meshopt_optimizeMeshletLevel with level 1+ (~0.5% gains)
  • Fix reduced encoding precision of small numbers when using meshopt_encodeFilterExp with a shared exponent mode if the input contains exact zeroes
  • Support special meshlet hardware configurations that require a limited triangle index span via MESHOPTIMIZER_CLUSTERIZER_INDEXLIMIT define
  • Support direct decoding of vertex data into destination buffer via MESHOPTIMIZER_VERTEXCODEC_ZEROCOPY define for slightly faster decoding (disabled by default as it does not work well with write-combined memory)

Additional improvements

  • clusterlod.h now implements DAG BVH construction via clodBuildHierarchy for efficient hierarchical cut selection
  • Add tangent generation to gltfpack when requested via -gt argument
  • Add experimental MeshoptTangents JavaScript module with the new tangent space generator
  • Fix meshopt_decoder.js Wasm SIMD implementation corner case when using v1 format and highest compression (part of 1.1.1 patch release)
  • Fix a rare race condition in meshopt_decoder.js when using WebWorkers via useWorkers (part of 1.1.1 patch release)
  • Improve vertex decoding performance in meshopt_decoder.js by 5-10%
  • Fix several bugs in gltfpack (mesh merging with negative scales no longer flips tangent frames, more careful handling of animation tracks with zero scale)
Commits
  • 9d9890c Merge pull request #1061 from zeux/nextver
  • f25b85a vertexcodec: Make decode static inline to fix linkage on internal tables
  • b3abb71 Update README.md
  • da13ccf meshletcodec: Mark all encode/decode APIs as stable
  • 730bba9 js: Update README.md
  • 98d9c98 js: Update Wasm binaries and versions everywhere
  • 32be568 Update version to v1.2 everywhere
  • c332fbb js: Fix reference decoder handling of target array with an offset
  • 1082dd4 js: Use stricter and more consistent definition for generateTangents
  • b2faaa1 Update README.md
  • Additional commits viewable in compare view

items.title: P0.1: Fix Case 2 threshold selection to use a validation split
items.body:
## Summary
Second of four "P0 hardening" sub-projects before v1.0.0. Fixes a real data-leakage bug flagged by an external audit: Case 2 Lesson 6 ("Threshold Selection and Metric Choice") previously chose its classification decision threshold by comparing precision/recall/F1 for 0.5/0.3/0.2 **directly on the test set** — reusing the test set for a tuning decision.

- Adds `split_for_validation(train_df) -> (fit_df, val_df)`, carved from `train_df` using the same convention as the existing split.
- The three-threshold comparison now happens on `val_df` (model fit on `fit_df`), not `test_df`.
- A new final notebook cell refits on the *full* `train_df` and reveals the one-time `test_df` check at the chosen threshold — the single legitimate touch of the test set.
- Investigation before writing any code found the actual blast radius was much smaller than the audit implied: Lessons 5, 7, 8 needed **zero code changes**. Lesson 7's risk tiers use fixed, unrelated probability cutoffs; Lesson 8's `final_scorecard` already fit its model on the full `train_df`, so its existing numbers were never wrong — only the *reasoning* that arrived at threshold 0.2 was leaky. Verified: the fixed Lesson 6's final reveal reproduces Lesson 8's existing numbers exactly (precision 0.24444444444444444, recall 0.55, f1 0.3384615384615385).
- Updates Lesson 6's README (both languages) and the already-merged Case 2 exemplar decision note, which had explicitly named this exact issue as a limitation — that limitation bullet is now marked resolved, and (caught during review) two other spots in the exemplar that still described/praised the old leaky methodology were also fixed for internal consistency.

- [x] `uv run ruff check .` → clean

- [x] Every hardcoded number in `check.py` independently re-derived from `solution.py`, not just trusted from its own passing assertions

- [x] Final whole-branch review: confirmed Lessons 5/7/8 genuinely untouched (`git diff --stat` scoped exactly to Lesson 6 + the exemplar note), re-verified the central "refit on full train_df reproduces Lesson 8's numbers" claim fresh

items.title: Complete Week 5: Quantization vs Quality (Phase II)
items.body:
## Summary

- Builds a full evaluation pipeline — `llama-server`-based runner, category-specific scorers (classification, extraction, structured output, summarization, reasoning, instruction-following), and statistical analysis (bootstrap CIs, paired effect sizes, failure-category breakdown) — and scores all six Week 4 quantization levels (F16 → Q3_K_M) against the 100-example evaluation dataset (600 generations).
- **Key finding:** quality does not decline monotonically with quantization. No level differs significantly from F16 down to Q4_K_M (Q6_K even scores nominally highest); only Q3_K_M shows a real, borderline-significant drop. Quality loss is highly category-dependent (`classification`/`structured_output` are robust, `information_extraction`/`instruction_following` degrade sharply at Q3_K_M) and includes a striking non-monotonic failure mode: Q4_K_M answers 7/8 Italian summarization prompts in English, while its higher- and lower-precision neighbors don't.
- Joining this week's quality numbers with Week 4's decode-speed numbers produces a two-point Pareto frontier: **Q6_K** (best quality, ~1.9x F16 speed) and **Q4_K_M** (fastest, quality indistinguishable from F16) — every other level is dominated on both axes by at least one of these two.
- A first evaluation pass surfaced three real prompt/scorer bugs (classification not showing the model its label set, reasoning scorer grabbing the first number instead of the last, information_extraction requiring exact key names it was never prompted for); all three were fixed and the full 600-generation run was repeated from scratch — documented in the README's limitations section as a methodology lesson, not hidden.
- Updates root README status table, the Week 5 glossary section, and the open-questions tracker (closes Q16, adds Q18-21).

items.title: Fix 7: Threat model document for security researchers
items.body:
v0.1 had no formal statement of what attacks `agentic-guard` claims to catch, what it explicitly does not, or what attacker capabilities the analyzer assumes. Security researchers look for this first; its absence reads as unprincipled. Fix 7 adds [`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`](docs/THREAT_MODEL.md) — a 467-line structured threat model addressed to OWASP contributors, academic researchers, and engineers evaluating the tool for their toolchain.

## Read first

- **[`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`](docs/THREAT_MODEL.md)** — the document itself.

## What's in the document

Ten sections, mapped to what a careful reviewer wants to know:

1. **Scope** — static-analysis / design-time framing; explicit "no execution, no LLM calls, no network."
2. **Position in the agent-security ecosystem** — a table contrasting `agentic-guard` against runtime classifiers (Lakera, NeMo Guardrails, Prompt Armor), runtime sandboxes (LlamaFirewall, Microsoft Prompt Shields), formal verification (TAINTAWI), and human-in-the-loop. The point: no single layer is sufficient; we make the architectural-review layer cheap.
3. **What we defend against** — IG001 (confused-deputy), IG002 (dynamic prompts), IG003 (library-call sinks, planned), IG004 (architectural leaks, planned), each with OWASP LLM Top 10 mapping and a concrete attack example.
4. **What we explicitly do NOT defend against** — ten enumerated classes: direct injection, jailbreaking, training-data poisoning, supply chain, multimodal adversarial, runtime-only attacks, side channels, DoS, model extraction, privacy leakage from training data.
5. **Attacker capability assumptions** — six capabilities granted, four denied, with the "LLM treated as adversarially-routed" framing called out as the strongest and most important assumption (this is the conceptual move that makes the whole approach defensible).
6. **Defender capability assumptions** — what the analyzer requires of its user.
7. **Coverage limitations** — ten known gaps, each cross-referenced to the rule, design doc, or future-PR plan that closes (or doesn't close) it.
8. **Comparison to adjacent threat models** — OWASP LLM Top 10, LlamaFirewall, TAINTAWI, Microsoft Prompt Shields, Simon Willison's prompt-injection writing.
9. **Threat-model evolution / versioning** — a protocol commitment that coverage claims and limitations are updated together so the document never drifts ahead of the implementation.
10. **Reporting a threat-model gap** — issue-template-style guidance for inbound reports.

## Acceptance criteria

From the Fix 7 brief:

- [x] **File exists at `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`** — 467 lines.
- [x] **README links to it prominently** — directly under the existing `HOW_IT_WORKS.md` reference, addressed to "Security researchers and OWASP contributors."
- [x] **`HOW_IT_WORKS.md` links to it from the "limitations" section** — blockquote at the top of "Honest limitations" distinguishing implementation-level limitations (HOW_IT_WORKS.md's scope) from conceptual coverage (THREAT_MODEL.md's scope).

## Self-consistency check

The document explicitly cites limitations that map to other v0.2 work in flight (IG003 library-call rule, IG004 architectural leaks, PR #5 function-local literal binding, CrewAI/MCP parsers). Each forward reference is honest about implementation status — "planned" entries are clearly labeled and tied to roadmap items, not presented as shipped.

The §9 versioning protocol commits to updating §3 coverage entries and §7 limitations together when new rules land. This prevents the document from making coverage claims that drift ahead of the implementation — the exact failure mode the v0.1 README had (claiming "real-world validation" with no public corpus or precision numbers).

## What's NOT in this PR

- No code changes. Pure documentation.
- No new tests. (67 pre-existing pass.)
- No new runtime dependencies.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/` — 67/67 pass (no source changes, defensive run)
- [x] `ruff check src tests` — clean (no source changes)
- [x] Markdown renders correctly on GitHub (links resolve; tables render; blockquote in HOW_IT_WORKS.md renders).
- [x] Internal cross-references (`§3.1`, `§7.5`, etc.) resolve when read top-to-bottom.

Updates `nanasess/bcmath-polyfill` from 1.0.2 to 1.1.0
Release notes

Sourced from nanasess/bcmath-polyfill's releases.

v1.1.0

This release completes PHP 8.4 bcmath compatibility. It adds bcdivmod(), implements all eight RoundingMode cases (including the directional modes), and reworks rounding to use exact arbitrary-precision string arithmetic — fixing a precision bug and significantly improving performance. Interoperability with symfony/polyfill-php84 is now documented.

✨ Added

  • bcdivmod() — returns the quotient and remainder of a division in a single call (PHP 8.4). It is built on arbitrary-precision division, so it works without the native bcmath extension (unlike symfony/polyfill-php84, which delegates to native bc). (#39)
  • All four directional RoundingMode cases for bcround(): TowardsZero, AwayFromZero, PositiveInfinity, and NegativeInfinity, alongside the existing four half-modes. (#36)

🐛 Fixed

  • Exact HalfEven / HalfOdd rounding. bcround() no longer falls back to a floating-point path, so results stay correct for large and high-precision numbers. Previously, digits beyond IEEE-754 precision were corrupted — e.g. bcround('12345678901234567890.5', 0, RoundingMode::HalfEven) returned 12345678901234567168 instead of 12345678901234567890.
  • Extremely large negative $precision values no longer risk excessive memory allocation when the result is zero.

🔧 Changed

  • Rounding rewritten as pure string-digit arithmetic (no BigInteger in the rounding path). It now matches native bcround() across every mode and precision, and makes bcround() / bcceil() roughly 5–6× faster.
  • RoundingMode is now a pure enum, matching native PHP 8.4 (no backing value; ->value, from() and tryFrom() are unavailable). This enum was not part of any previous release, so no released code is affected.

⚠️ Minor compatibility note

  • The parameter name of bcfloor() / bcceil() / bcround() changed from $operand to $num, to match the native signature. Positional calls are unaffected (e.g. bcround('1.5', 2)); only named-argument calls need updating: bcround(operand: '1.5') → bcround(num: '1.5').

🤝 Interoperability with symfony/polyfill-php84

symfony/polyfill-php84 declares the same PHP 8.4 bc functions, but only when the native bcmath extension is already loaded. When both packages are installed on PHP 8.2/8.3 with the extension, either implementation may win depending on autoload order (guarded by function_exists(), so there is no fatal redeclaration). Because this package now uses a native-compatible string algorithm, the numeric results are identical in either case. See the README for details.

🧪 Internal / CI

  • Enabled 8 previously-skipped official php-src PHPT tests across PHP 8.1–8.5: bcdivmod, bcdivmod_by_zero, bcround_all, bcround_away_from_zero, bcround_ceiling, bcround_floor, bcround_toward_zero, and bcround_early_return.

Refs #81 · Closes #36 · Closes #39

Full Changelog: https://github.com/nanasess/bcmath-polyfill/compare/1.0.3...1.1.0

v1.0.3

What's Changed

🐛 Bug Fixes

Fix Rector 2.4+ scoped polyfill collision with RoundingMode (#56, #57)

Prior releases failed with a fatal error in environments that dev-require rector/rector: ^2.4:

PHP Fatal error:  Cannot declare enum RoundingMode, because the name is already
in use in /path/to/vendor/nanasess/bcmath-polyfill/lib/RoundingMode.php on line 16

Rector 2.4.0+ ships a scoped polyfill (vendor/rector/rector/vendor/symfony/polyfill-php84/Resources/RoundingMode.php) that declares a global class RoundingMode via class_alias on PHP < 8.4. The previous guard !enum_exists('RoundingMode') could not detect a preexisting class definition, so the polyfill tried to declare its enum on top of the class and crashed.

The guard was rewritten to !class_exists('RoundingMode', false), which correctly detects both:

  • The native PHP 8.4+ RoundingMode enum (enums are reported as classes by class_exists() since PHP 8.1)
  • Classes aliased into the global namespace by third-party scoped polyfills (Rector 2.4+, etc.)

The second argument false prevents autoload from triggering, so third-party stub files are not accidentally executed.

items.title: AW-0011 Ponytail precision + pack v0.5.0
items.body:
## What

- Imports **two** rules from Ponytail into `templates/AGENTS.template.md`:
  - **Edge-case tiebreaker** — "lazy means less code, not a flimsier algorithm": between two same-size stdlib options, take the edge-case-correct one.
  - **No-prose-defense** — if the explanation of a simplification runs longer than the code, delete the explanation and mark the corner with `SHORTCUT(…)` instead.
- Enriches the anti-abstraction clause with concrete examples (no interface with one impl, no factory for one product, no config for an unchanging value).
- Records in ADR-0011 the **hooks precision** (the declined Ponytail hooks do context-injection + a statusline badge only — no PreToolUse/PostToolUse, no enforcement) and the **performance-claims precision** (Ponytail's headline numbers are single-shot Claude-only and explicitly disclaimed upstream for agentic, cross-lineage use).

## Why

A 2026-06-17 ground-truth read of the real Ponytail repo showed the hooks we declined under AW-0001 do **context-injection only, not enforcement** — so declining them forgoes ergonomics, not an enforcement mechanism, making the AW-0001 decline cleaner. The same read confirmed upstream **disclaims** its performance figures for agentic, multi-turn, non-Claude use — so we must not claim them. Both facts belong in the decision record; the two cherry-picked rules are real gaps worth importing.

## Tier: `medium`

Governance / decision-record surface (per the AW-0004 risk floor) — ships via PR with cross-lineage review before a human merges. **This PR does NOT merge.**

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---
**Update — pack version bump (v0.3.7 → v0.5.0).** This PR also bumps `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` to `0.5.0` (a deliberate jump past 0.4), since it changes baseline content (the two imported rules) — v0.5.0 is the version consuming repos pin to for it. Illustrative `e.g. v0.3.7` stamps in AW-0007, `docs/adr/README.md`, and `AGENTS.template.md` refreshed to `v0.5.0`.

Updates `meshoptimizer` from 1.1.1 to 1.2.0
Release notes

Sourced from meshoptimizer's releases.

v1.2

This release introduces a major new feature, tangent frame generation, significantly improves vertex decoding performance on Intel/AMD CPUs and also adds several smaller features and improvements. Highlights:

A new tangent frame generator can generate tangents from either indexed or unindexed triangle mesh with positions/normals/texture coordinates. The generator implements MikkTSpace algorithm, but is significantly faster to run (~6-10x faster than mikktspace.c depending on the input structure). Note that the generation result is a per-corner tangent and applying the tangents to the indexed mesh may require splitting source vertices; consult documentation for details. By default, the algorithm uses a modified weighting scheme that significantly improves tangent quality around beveled regions in the mesh, with meshopt_TangentCompatible option provided for cases where exact compatibility with mikktspace.c is important (e.g. normal map baking workflows).

Vertex decoding (meshopt_decodeVertexBuffer) implementation for Intel/AMD CPUs has been significantly revised. The new mostly branchless SSSE3 implementation is usually ~20-45% faster than it was in previous releases, with the gains depending on CPU and the data composition; it's typical to see gains in the upper half of this range for engine-packed data. This implementation is automatically selected on compatible CPUs (SSSE3+POPCNT), with no change in data encoding, so to get this performance boost a library update is sufficient. If the code is compiled with AVX-512/AVX10 support (which is currently only selected at compile time when opted into), the decoding is an additional ~10% faster.

Additionally, new index filtering functions are provided to remove degenerate/duplicate triangles based on positional identity, which can be especially helpful for raytracing performance, a function for computing optimal shared exponent for cluster positions can be used to prepare geometry for upcoming DXR2 Compressed1 format, and clusterlod.h now implements DAG BVH construction via clodBuildHierarchy.

The majority of the work on the core library in this release has been sponsored by Valve; thank you!

Library improvements

  • New experimental function for generating tangents based on MikkTSpace algorithm, meshopt_generateTangents
  • New experimental functions for filtering out degenerate and duplicate triangles based on positional identity, meshopt_filterIndexBuffer/meshopt_filterIndexBufferMulti
  • New experimental function for computing optimal shared exponent for cluster positions which can be used with upcoming DXR2 Compressed1 format
  • meshopt_encode/decodeMeshlet* functions, meshopt_extractMeshletIndices and meshopt_optimizeMeshletLevel functions, as well as meshopt_SimplifyVertex_Priority and meshopt_SimplifyRegularizeLight flags, are now stable.
  • Significantly improve meshopt_decodeVertexBuffer performance on existing data for Intel/AMD CPUs (20-45% faster depending on CPU and data characteristics)
  • Significantly improve performance of meshopt_partitionClusters on larger partition sizes (~2x for target_size 64, ~200x for 1024)
  • Improve post-compression ratio for meshlets encoded using meshlet codec after meshopt_optimizeMeshletLevel with level 1+ (~0.5% gains)
  • Fix reduced encoding precision of small numbers when using meshopt_encodeFilterExp with a shared exponent mode if the input contains exact zeroes
  • Support special meshlet hardware configurations that require a limited triangle index span via MESHOPTIMIZER_CLUSTERIZER_INDEXLIMIT define
  • Support direct decoding of vertex data into destination buffer via MESHOPTIMIZER_VERTEXCODEC_ZEROCOPY define for slightly faster decoding (disabled by default as it does not work well with write-combined memory)

Additional improvements

  • clusterlod.h now implements DAG BVH construction via clodBuildHierarchy for efficient hierarchical cut selection
  • Add tangent generation to gltfpack when requested via -gt argument
  • Add experimental MeshoptTangents JavaScript module with the new tangent space generator
  • Fix meshopt_decoder.js Wasm SIMD implementation corner case when using v1 format and highest compression (part of 1.1.1 patch release)
  • Fix a rare race condition in meshopt_decoder.js when using WebWorkers via useWorkers (part of 1.1.1 patch release)
  • Improve vertex decoding performance in meshopt_decoder.js by 5-10%
  • Fix several bugs in gltfpack (mesh merging with negative scales no longer flips tangent frames, more careful handling of animation tracks with zero scale)

items.title: Number-classifier precision: degradation augmentation + abstain class (task G)
items.body:
## Summary

D-4/E-1 proved **read precision** is the identity wall: the D-3 classifier collapsed small in-game numbers onto "22" (113 of 339 reads, 33%), and stitching (E-1) couldn't fix a classifier that mislabels. Root cause is a **domain gap** — D-3 trained on curated readable 224² crops, but a live crop is a ~12-17 px number box upscaled to 224 and motion-blurred. No new labelled data is available ($0 rule), so precision comes from the model.

## Two levers, zero new manual labels

- **Degradation augmentation** (`scripts/train_number_classifier.py`) mirrors the deploy pipeline: training crops randomly downscaled to ~20-48 px then back to 224 + motion-blurred.
- **"unreadable" abstain class** — the model rejects a crop instead of guessing. Seeds = the 52 empty-label OCR crops; the rest are **mined free** from `basketball-player-detection-3` (torso patches of players whose number box wasn't detected). `identify_players.py` drops abstain reads from voting.

`--no-degrade --no-abstain` reproduces the D-3 model; `--eval-only WEIGHTS` scores any checkpoint on the same tiers.

## Held-out (new vs old v0.5.0)

| tier | old | new |
|---|---|---|
| clean number acc | 0.955 | 0.949 |
| **degraded number acc** | 0.859 | **0.952** |
| **abstain recall** | n/a | **0.889** |

## On the clip (same 30 s window, same code path, old → new)

| metric | old | new |
|---|---|---|
| "22" read share | 113/339 (33%) | 18/248 (**7%**) |
| reads rejected as unreadable | 0 | **91** |
| distinct players named | 4 (`0,11,22,30`) | **6** (`0,9,11,30,34,42`) |
| max same-number tracks | 3 | 2 |
| read rate | 0.113 | **0.151** |

The pathological "#22 on three concurrent players" is gone; the classifier now rejects 91 garbage crops and surfaces a realistic spread of distinct numbers.

## Honest limit

This improves precision *behaviour* — no collapse, abstains on garbage — but **without a roster / ground truth we can't verify each named number is the true player** (jerseys aren't hand-legible on this 720p pan), and read rate is still ~15%. Ships as the same honest hybrid, now with a materially cleaner identity signal. The demo sample + `docs/player_identity_nba.json` regenerate with the new model; the app's honesty note reflects the abstain step.

Weights = [release v0.6.0](https://github.com/seungminnam/hoop-vision/releases/tag/v0.6.0). ADR-012; README/ROADMAP/reference-analysis updated. ruff clean; **132 tests pass**.

items.title: docs: close out cmc-phalanx-canonicalize spec — demote Phalanx, add shingled-extraction deep-dive
items.body:
## Summary

Closes out the remaining action items from `docs/cleanup/cmc-phalanx-canonicalize.md` (the naming-cleanup coordination doc on main). Audit found 5 spec items still pending; this PR lands all of them so the coordination doc can be retired in a follow-up alongside `docs/cleanup/`.

The spec's three locked decisions are now enforced across all in-scope surfaces:

- **A** — Phalanx (system) · CMC-Lite (spec) · canonicalize (module): three names, three audiences
- **B** — Phalanx is the **resolver only**; shingled extraction is a **separate primitive** with its own deep-dive
- **C** — Phalanx stays **out of marketing surfaces** (root README, getting-started, zeitghost — that last already done in zeitghost PR #4)

## What lands

- **`README.md`** — 8 Phalanx mentions in the top-level pitch all demoted to plain descriptive language ("the resolver", "Entity Resolution"). Stale `≥85% recall` stat (which was the **full CMC pipeline's target**, never a CMC-Lite measured guarantee) replaced with the precision-first measured numbers from PR #58: **100% auto-merge precision, 0 false merges across 5 corpora, 100% drift surfaced for review**. Same framing as the merged zeitghost landing copy, so the story is consistent across surfaces.

- **`docs/entity-resolution.md`** — H1 stripped of "— Phalanx"; opening leads with "Entity resolution in spiritwriter works by defining fields, not surface forms" per the spec's wording suggestion. Phalanx stays in the body as the system name (deep-dive surface, where it's earned).

- **`docs/getting-started.md`** — same Phalanx demotion in the Entity Resolution section. Top-of-funnel, treated as marketing-adjacent.

- **`docs/shingled-extraction.md`** (NEW) — the deep-dive the zeitghost homepage entry ix points at. Covers the overlapping-window + multi-pass-consensus pattern, when to use vs not, the why-shingled naming note, and a tour of the reference implementation at `examples/extract_memory.py`.
